extracted.intended_audience: historians and philosophers of science, science educators, and scholars interested in the epistemology and organization of research practice
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing how research problems, problem-solving strategies, and laboratory practices are transmitted across generations of scientists and how that transmission affects scientific productivity, consensus, and refinement. Includes historical examples (e.g., Liebig) and mechanisms of pedagogy and lab organization.

rubrics_metrics.name: Undergraduate curriculum transmits problem families
rubrics_metrics.description: The undergraduate science curriculum acquaints students with general families of problems (e.g., problems of motion, fields) so they develop a sense for the fundamental character of research problems in a field.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This early exposure helps budding scientists recognize and independently formulate novel research problems that fit naturally within the field; general characteristics are acquired first and serve as a scaffold for more specific structures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized formal training narrows applicability
rubrics_metrics.description: More specialized formal techniques have narrow ranges of application; students trained in advanced formal approaches face limited opportunities to use them outside intended problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Continued use of advanced approaches requires and promotes the continued relevance of the sorts of problems to which those approaches have historically been applied; specialization thereby stabilizes problem types across generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specialized experimental training and model-systems bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Graduate and postdoc experimental training (technologies, model organisms) equips scientists with highly specialized knowledge that does not easily export to unrelated problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Due to this, new scientists often pursue problems similar to those they were trained on; experimental specialization reinforces reproduction of existing problem types.

rubrics_metrics.name: Assignment of dissertation topics stabilizes problem sets
rubrics_metrics.description: In many natural sciences, graduate students are assigned to labs and given thesis problems that fit into the PI's ongoing research program, rather than freely choosing novel topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This direct assignment is a powerful mechanism by which research problems are transmitted from veterans to apprentices, stabilizing the set of problems the community adapts to over generations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division of problem-solving strategies: formal vs experimental
rubrics_metrics.description: Problem-solving strategies inherited through undergraduate education divide into (1) formal techniques and (2) experimental techniques, each transmitted differently.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal techniques are primarily trained via problem sets and exercises that teach association of problem type with technique; experimental techniques are typically transmitted experientially and tacitly through apprenticeship.

rubrics_metrics.name: Problem sets train reflexive association of problems and methods
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of problem sets in textbooks trains students to see certain problems as the kinds for which particular formal approaches are used (e.g., trigonometry for mechanics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students who excel instantly identify problem types and apply the appropriate manipulative technique; this ensures those who proceed to advanced training have internalized central problem-solving strategies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tacit knowledge requires master-apprentice transmission
rubrics_metrics.description: Experimental procedures often require high-bandwidth, tacit knowledge that is difficult to articulate and is more faithfully transmitted through experiential master-apprentice relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although experimental methods are described in articles, successful execution often depends on tacit skills that cannot be achieved through purely verbal channels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ahistorical/uncritical pedagogy preserves fidelity
rubrics_metrics.description: An ahistorical and otherwise uncritical mode of undergraduate training (described by Kuhn as 'pedagogically unexceptionable') promotes high-fidelity transmission of problem-solving strategies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimizing opportunities for critical reflection helps students internalize dogmatic, reflexive responses to problem types, which enhances efficiency in 'normal science' though it may limit critical understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Simplicity and precision (content bias) promote diffusion
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods that are sufficiently simple and precise (a 'content bias') are easy to copy and diffuse widely (e.g., Liebig's Kaliapparat).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Simple methods level the experimental playing field, allowing novices to achieve reliable results by reading descriptions; rapid diffusion follows when novices do not need personal instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods that give clear signals of trial quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Techniques that provide plentiful, easily-interpretable signals indicating whether a trial is good or bad (e.g., bubble behavior, fluid level changes, color changes) allow operators to distinguish usable from bad data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These signals function as feedback mechanisms for optimization and as indicators of failure that tell the operator when to discard data and repeat trials; this increases precision, accuracy, and uniformity of results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ability to sort good from bad data increases uniformity
rubrics_metrics.description: The ease with which good data can be identified and bad data discarded improves the precision and uniformity of results across practitioners.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Coupled with simplicity, this makes methods copyable by a broad population and reduces variance among independent practitioners' results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decomposition of training into components with assessment
rubrics_metrics.description: Breaking analytic training into well-defined stages and using formal assessments (e.g., frequent exams) ensures students acquire requisite knowledge and skills.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decomposition allows instructors to identify specific obstacles preventing a student from reaching competence and to guarantee proficiency in relevant aspects before independent work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Charismatic leadership as a copying incentive
rubrics_metrics.description: Charismatic leaders (e.g., Liebig) inspire loyalty that encourages students to emulate and faithfully follow instructions, increasing diligence and effort in copying practices.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any mechanism that increases rewards for copying will tend to increase copying rates; charisma is one such mechanism that indirectly raises problem-solving throughput.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of student assignments: gap-filling vs novel projects
rubrics_metrics.description: Labs assign (1) gap-filling exercises closely related to prior work and training, which maximize replication, and (2) qualitatively novel projects clustered around the PI's concerns, which introduce directed variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gap-filling exhausts resources exploitable by existing methods; novel projects attempt to expand the environment and the set of exploitables, balancing fidelity and innovation in scientific evolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor- and complexity-driven decomposition of problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems that become sufficiently complex or labor-intensive must be decomposed into smaller projects distributed across many individuals; such decomposition makes problems good at copying themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Once a problem exceeds an individual's capacity, distribution and decomposition enable collective effort and propagation of problem-types across generations of researchers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Standardization + ease of use leads to consensus
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardization of methods narrows disagreement only when the standardized method is easy to use and copy; standardization alone is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When everyone uses an easy, reliably copyable method, independent practitioners are likely to obtain similar results, accelerating consensus (e.g., organic composition estimates after Kaliapparat diffusion).

rubrics_metrics.name: High-fidelity copying enables taking things for granted
rubrics_metrics.description: Widespread copying of practices and consensus permits practitioners to take certain facts, representations, and approaches for granted, freeing resources for deeper inquiry and refinement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This permission to take items as given characterizes 'normal science' and underpins the community's ability to progress via directional refinement.
